title: Linear Light, Self-Sizing Frames, Outlined Type, Intent & Streamed Slots
description: Canvas that sums light not bytes, iframes sized in CSS, strokes behind fills, browser-timed hover intent, and out-of-order slots.

drops.title: Additive Light, Done in Linear
drops.description: The same nine emitters summed twice — once as encoded sRGB bytes, once as actual light — rendered side by side.
drops.concept: Light adds linearly; sRGB numbers do not, so 'lighter' compositing on an ordinary canvas blows overlaps out to flat white and shifts their hue. Chrome 155 adds srgb-linear and display-p3-linear to PredefinedColorSpace, letting a 2D canvas composite in linear light. Both halves here run identical geometry through identical code; the only difference is whether the transfer function is applied before the sum or after it, and a ×6 difference view maps exactly where the error lives.
drops.source: WICG canvas-color-space proposal (the spec work behind Chrome 155's new colour spaces)

interaction.mouse: Drag exposure, radius and emitter count to push the overlaps further apart.
interaction.click: Switch scenes (spotlights / bloom / ramp) or flip to the amplified difference view.
interaction.touch: All controls are sliders and buttons in the glass panel; the canvas is decorative.

drops.title: Iframes That Hug Their Content
drops.description: frame-sizing: content-height on the parent plus one opt-in meta in the child deletes the postMessage resize dance.
drops.concept: Embedding a widget has always meant guessing a height and then patching it with a measure-and-postMessage loop. Chrome 154 moves it into CSS: the embedding page sets frame-sizing: content-height and the embedded document opts in with <meta name="responsive-embedded-sizing">. Three real srcdoc iframes grow and shrink on demand, with one card deliberately left on a fixed 110px box so you can watch it clip.
drops.source: Chrome for Developers — “Responsive iframes in Chrome 154”

interaction.mouse: Add and remove paragraphs and watch each frame re-fit; the readout prints the live frame height.
interaction.click: Grow / shrink / reset drive the embedded documents.
interaction.touch: Buttons are full-size tap targets; the grid collapses to one column.

drops.title: Outlines That Don't Eat the Letters
drops.description: -webkit-text-stroke draws half its width inward; paint-order: stroke fill pushes it behind the fill so it only grows outward.
drops.concept: Heavy text strokes quietly destroy letterforms — counters close, thin joins vanish — because half the stroke is painted over the glyph. paint-order: stroke fill reverses the order so the fill always sits on top. Chromium picked the property up for HTML text, so the old workaround of duplicating the text into a pseudo-element is gone. Two identical words at identical stroke widths make the difference impossible to miss as you drag the slider.
drops.source: MDN paint-order reference, alongside Tyler Sticka's “Improved CSS Text-Stroke” (Aug 2026)

interaction.mouse: Drag the stroke width; the left specimen closes up while the right one stays legible.
interaction.click: Swap stroke and fill colours, including a transparent fill for a hollow cut.
interaction.touch: The control panel docks to the bottom of the screen on small viewports.

drops.title: Interest, Not Hover
drops.description: interestfor plus :interest-source and :interest-target hand enter, leave and long-press timing to the browser.
drops.concept: A hover card is three problems — enter, leave, and the forgiving gap between them — and every implementation rebuilds the same timers. The Interest Invoker API makes it declarative: interestfor points at any element by id, two pseudo-classes style both ends, and interest-delay-start / interest-delay-end tune the intent threshold in CSS. Five cards sit over live prose with the delays exposed as sliders, and the JS fallback shows exactly how much code the feature deletes.

interaction.mouse: Hover any highlighted term; raise the show delay and the intent threshold becomes obvious.
interaction.click: Clicking or focusing a term opens its card too — the same invoker handles all three.
interaction.touch: Tap a term to summon its card; tap elsewhere or press Escape to dismiss.

drops.title: Markup That Streams In
drops.description: Skeleton slots that a later <template for> replaces, plus the new insertion family ending in streamAppendHTML().
drops.concept: Out-of-order streaming — send the shell now, fill the slow slots whenever the data lands — is moving out of frameworks and into the parser. A slot is marked with <?start>/<?end> around its fallback, and a <template for="id"> later in the same response swaps it in place. The JS half is a consistent insertion family: setHTML, appendHTML, replaceWithHTML and streaming counterparts like streamAppendHTML(), which returns a WritableStream. The slowest card here resolves last on purpose, and the log prints arrival order against document order.
drops.source: InfoQ — “Out-of-Order HTML Streaming Moves from JS Frameworks into the Browser”

interaction.mouse: Hit stream and watch four slots resolve in arrival order, not document order.
interaction.click: Stream and reset re-run the whole choreography with a fresh timing log.
interaction.touch: Cards stack to one column; the log scrolls independently.
